independent_physics.retarded_time: lighttime.retarded iterates s = |x_obs - x_src(t - s)| / c four times from s = 0 with the observer fixed at the observation time, in the galactic frame about the game origin (translation-invariant). This is the correct retarded-time equation for the rest-frame image at the ship's event; (v/c)^4 < 2e-15 of the lag remains, far below the 1e-6 s tolerance. rel_km uses r.pos (the source at t_r); the pole and W use r.time; light_age_s = lagDays x 86400. The ship's velocity is not used anywhere, as the design requires. The retarded offset for Jupiter at opposition is 26,000 km (v x lag), asserted in celestial_test.ail:372-382 and killed by the no-retardation mutant.
independent_physics.time_scale: system.jd = epoch_jd + t x 365.25 (celestial.ail:54-55). t is M2's galaxy-frame clock in Julian years (core.ail uses medium.julianYearS = 365.25 x 86400 s for every energy integral, so the sim is self-consistent). The ephemeris argument is TDB; TDB - TT <= 1.7 ms, which moves the Moon 2 m. The only labelling question is TT vs UTC when a scenario epoch is written from a calendar date (69 s in 2023, i.e. 70 km for the Moon and 900 km for Jupiter, 0.2 arcsec from Earth): negligible for the game, worth one line in the scenario-parameter docs. The fixture confirms the arithmetic: t = 0.01 yr -> jd 2460255.1525 = 2460251.5 + 3.6525.
independent_physics.frames: eclipticToGalactic = Hipparcos A_G^T o Rx(epsilon_J2000). The matrix's third row equals (cos dG cos aG, cos dG sin aG, sin dG) to 10 digits and the first row equals the galactic-centre direction; the north ecliptic pole maps to l = 96.384, b = 29.811 deg (textbook 96.38, 29.81). The Sun's pole (RA 286.13, Dec 63.87) maps to (-0.0715730, 0.9192895, 0.3870195), which is the fixture's value. poleAndSpin returns the pole already in ecliptic J2000 and W in [0, 2 pi); stateGal rotates the pole once more to galactic (celestial.ail:85) and viewOf does the same at t_r (celestial.ail:123). The pole unit length is 1 +/- 4e-11 (the 10-digit matrix), tested at 1e-9: appropriate.
independent_physics.mean_orbit_label: ephemerisAt (celestial.ail:58-59) is inclusive on both window edges and agrees with elementsAt's meanOrbit flag at windowStart - 0.5, windowStart, J2000, windowEnd, windowEnd + 0.5 and J2000 + 1e6 yr (celestial_test.ail:389-390). earth_moon_barycentre.finding: Standish's Earth row is the Earth-Moon barycentre. moonHelio adds the geocentric Moon vector to it (celestial.ail:78-82), so the sim's Earth and Moon are both displaced from truth by +mu r_geo with mu = 1/82.3: 0.01215 x 384,400 km = 4,671 km, the PR's number. The Earth-Moon relative vector is exact.
earth_moon_barycentre.severity_for_the_50000_km_start: It depends entirely on how the ship is placed. If M5.5b/M5.7 place the ship via bodyAt('earth') (the only sensible way), the view from 50,000 km is self-consistent: the Earth is where the ship expects it, the Moon's direction is exact, and the residual errors are the Sun's direction (4,671 km / 1 AU = 6.4 arcsec) and the Earth's phase, both invisible. If anything ever places the ship in absolute coordinates (a saved game from a corrected build, an external ephemeris, the α Cen return leg computed against true Earth), the Earth disc (angular radius 6.5 deg at 56,378 km) would be displaced by up to atan(4671/56378) = 4.7 deg, a third of its diameter: glaring. There is also an honesty cost: anyone comparing the codex to Horizons sees Earth 0.73 Earth radii off.
earth_moon_barycentre.deferral_judgement: Right call. The fix is package maths (Earth = EMB - mu r_geo, Moon = EMB + (1 - mu) r_geo, with mu from the DE440 GMs already in the data) and gate 3 says it goes into sunholo/celestial first, with tests and a CHANGELOG, then the sim re-pins. Doing it inside sim/celestial.ail would have put a formula outside the package. Condition: the sprint plan's M5.5b and M5.7 rows should name celestial 0.1.1 as a dependency so it cannot slip past the start-at-Earth scene; today it is only an open_items entry in the sprint JSON.
earth_moon_barycentre.also_consider_in_0_1_1: The same split is not needed for the giant planets: Standish's Jupiter-Neptune rows are planet-system barycentres and the moons' mean elements are planetocentric, so the planets carry a barycentre offset too, but it is ~1,000 km for Jupiter (0.014 R_J, 0.3 arcsec at opposition) and less for the others; worth a one-line note in the package, not a change.
